questions.q: What question does AWS CloudTrail answer that CloudWatch metrics and logs cannot?
options: Who made a given API call against the account, and when
How much CPU an EC2 instance is currently using
How many bytes were written to an EBS volume in the last hour
What the current AWS bill total is
questions.explain: CloudTrail is AWS's control-plane audit log — it records who did what, and when, which metrics and logs were never designed to show.

options: An always-on, 90-day record of account activity, enabled automatically for every AWS account at no extra charge
A paid feature that must be manually enabled before any events are recorded
A record that only captures events from the last 24 hours
A feature exclusive to AWS Organizations accounts
questions.explain: Event History is on by default for every account, with no setup, recording the last 90 days of API activity.

questions.q: Why would an administrator create a CloudTrail Trail instead of relying only on Event History?
options: A Trail delivers log files continuously to an S3 bucket (optionally also CloudWatch Logs) for retention well beyond Event History's 90-day window
A Trail is required before any API calls can be made in the account
Event History only works for S3, never for EC2
Trails replace the need for IAM entirely
questions.explain: A Trail extends retention past 90 days and can deliver events to S3 or a CloudWatch Logs group, useful for compliance or longer-term auditing.

questions.q: What is the real difference between a management event and a data event in CloudTrail?
options: Management events are control-plane operations logged by default; data events are high-volume, object-level operations that must be turned on deliberately
Management events are never logged, only data events are
Data events only apply to IAM, never to S3 or Lambda
There is no practical difference between the two
questions.explain: Management events (like launching an instance) are logged by a Trail by default, while data events (like an S3 GetObject call) are higher-volume and opt-in.

questions.q: An EC2 instance stops unexpectedly and no one admits to stopping it. Which tool actually identifies who did it?
options: CloudTrail, by looking up the StopInstances API call and the identity that made it
CloudWatch metrics, since CPUUtilization will show who logged in
CloudWatch Dashboards, since they display user activity
SNS, since it tracks every account action automatically
questions.explain: Metrics can show the instance went to a stopped state, but only CloudTrail ties that action to the specific identity, timestamp, and source IP that caused it.
